part2Results.structuredChinese: 我想介绍一台对我很有意义的旧相机。它是我爸爸大约十年前送给我的，当时我刚开始对摄影感兴趣。相机本身并不昂贵，外形也很普通，机身上甚至有几道使用留下的划痕，但我一直很珍惜它。真正让我喜欢上这台相机，是几年前的一次海边旅行。那天我们为了看日出很早就出门，我用它拍下了天空从深蓝慢慢变成橙色的过程。因为它不像手机那样能马上看到照片，我只能更认真地观察光线和构图。后来冲洗出来的照片并不完美，有几张还有点模糊，但那种等待结果的感觉很特别。现在我平时更多用手机拍照，因为确实方便得多，不过偶尔拿起这台旧相机时，我还是会想起那次旅行，也会提醒自己放慢一点，认真看看眼前的东西。

part2Results.spokenEnglish: I'd like to talk about an old camera that means a lot to me. My dad gave it to me about ten years ago, right when I was first getting into photography. The camera itself wasn't expensive and it looks pretty ordinary — there are even a few scratches on the body from years of use — but I've always treasured it. What really made me fall in love with it was a trip to the coast a few years back. We'd gone out really early that morning to catch the sunrise, and I used it to capture the sky changing from deep blue to orange. Because you can't instantly check your shots like you can on a phone, I had to pay much closer attention to the light and the composition. When the photos came back from being developed, they weren't perfect — a couple were even a bit blurry — but there was something really special about that whole process of waiting to see how they'd turned out. These days I mostly use my phone for photos since it's just so much more convenient, but every now and then when I pick up that old camera, I'm taken right back to that morning by the sea. It also reminds me to slow down a bit and really look at what's in front of me.

part2Results.structuredChinese: 我想说的一项实用技能是做饭，尤其是做一碗简单但味道不错的面。以前我几乎不会做饭，忙的时候经常随便点外卖。后来有一个假期，我跟家里人学了最基本的步骤，比如怎么调汤底、什么时候放蔬菜，以及怎样让面条保持合适的口感。刚开始我总是手忙脚乱，有时汤太咸，有时面又煮得太软，但练了几次以后，我慢慢找到了自己的节奏。现在如果学习或工作了一整天，我会给自己做一碗面，加上鸡蛋和冰箱里现有的蔬菜。整个过程可能只有二十分钟，却会让我从紧张的状态里安静下来。这项技能对我有用，不只是因为能省一点钱，也因为我可以根据自己的口味调整，而且偶尔还能做给朋友吃。它并不是什么了不起的本领，但确实让我的日常生活更独立、更舒服。

part2Results.spokenEnglish: The practical skill I'd like to talk about is cooking, or more specifically, making a simple but decent bowl of noodles. I used to be pretty hopeless in the kitchen — whenever things got busy, I'd just order takeout without thinking twice. Then one holiday, I learned the basics from my family: how to get the broth right, when to throw in the vegetables, and how to keep the noodles at that perfect texture. At first, I was all over the place — sometimes the soup would come out way too salty, other times I'd overcook the noodles until they were practically mush. But after a few tries, I gradually found my own rhythm. These days, if I've had a long day of studying or work, I'll make myself a bowl with an egg and whatever vegetables I've got in the fridge. The whole thing takes maybe twenty minutes, but it completely shifts me out of that tense, wound-up state. What makes this skill genuinely useful for me isn't just saving a bit of money — it's that I can adjust everything to my own taste, and every now and then I'll cook for a friend too. It's nothing particularly impressive, but it's made my day-to-day life feel more independent, more comfortable somehow.
